### 1.  Using \(0,\,1,\,2\equiv -1\)

Let a “non‑zero” entry be the value \(1\) or \(2\;(= -1)\)  
and a “zero” entry be the value \(3\;(=0\pmod3)\).
The conditions become

* (i) the number of \(2\)’s (\(-1\)’s) among the seven entries satisfies  
\[
n_1+2n_2\equiv0\pmod3. \tag{3}
\]

* (ii) a cyclic triple product is \(0\) iff at least one entry of the
triple is a zero.
Thus only those triples consisting entirely of non‑zeros contribute to \(T\).
If a contributing triple contains an odd number of \(2\)’s the product
is \(2\equiv-1\pmod3\) and if it contains an even number of \(2\)’s it is
\(1\pmod3\).

Let a “non‑zero block’’ be a maximal sequence of consecutive non‑zero
entries.  
If a block has length \(L\),

* it contributes \(L-2\) triples (unless \(L<3\) in which case it
contributes \(0\));
* each of these triples gives either \(1\) or \(2\pmod3\).

Because \(2\equiv-1\pmod3\) we can rewrite the contribution of a block

\[
\text{block contribution}\equiv (L-2)+\text{(number of triples in which the
product equals $2$)}\pmod3.\tag{4}
\]

(Equivalently the block’s contribution is the sum of
the signs \(+1\) (even number of \(2\)’s) and \(-1\) (odd number of
\(2\)’s).)

Let \(z\) be the number of zeros; hence \(n_0=z,\;n_1+n_2=7-z\).

\[

\[
